A HIV‑positive patient has undetectable viral load but persistent low CD4 count – which chromatin change may explain viral latency? — Identify heterochromatin formation at integration sites.
You lack access to ChIP; what alternative test can suggest abnormal histone modification in a suspected lymphoma? — Use methylation‑specific PCR as a surrogate.
Why might a patient on an HDAC inhibitor develop thrombocytopenia? — Explain off‑target effects on megakaryocyte gene expression.
During a ward round, you notice a patient on long‑term antimalarial therapy developing liver fibrosis – could epigenetic changes be involved? — Discuss drug‑induced histone acetylation alterations.
How does the 30‑nm fiber facilitate rapid DNA replication during fever spikes in malaria? — Relate loosened chromatin to increased transcription of heat‑shock proteins.
ai.title: DNA Tertiary Structure
ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: The tertiary structure of DNA describes how the double helix folds and packs inside the nucleus, influencing gene expression, replication and stability. Clinicians must recognise how alterations affect disease and how limited resources impact assessment.

b: Nucleosome: 147 bp DNA wrapped around a histone octamer
30‑nm fiber: stacked nucleosomes forming a solenoid
Loop‑domain: DNA attached to scaffold proteins, creating topologically associating domains (TADs)
sections.p: Beyond the double helix (secondary structure), DNA coils into nucleosomes, loops and higher‑order domains that fit within the cell nucleus. This folding regulates which genes are accessible for transcription.

Histone tails are chemically modified (acetylation, methylation) to loosen or tighten DNA packing, thereby turning genes on or off. In low‑resource settings, epigenetic changes can be driven by infections (e.g., malaria, HIV) and malnutrition.
Enzymes called writers, erasers and readers add, remove or interpret histone marks. ATP‑dependent remodelers slide nucleosomes to expose promoter regions.
Disrupted tertiary structure leads to inappropriate gene silencing or activation, contributing to cancer, developmental disorders and viral latency.
